paper_title: Mage-VL-Cowork: A Full Training Recipe to Learn Hybrid Computer Use From Evolved Harnesses

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Effective computer-use agents (CUAs) should seamlessly combine visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution within a single policy. We present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a general multimodally aligned checkpoint through an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum across midtraining, SFT, and RL. To power this curriculum at scale, Mage-CUA-Forge replaces per-task agent construction with reusable, skill-conditioned generation workflows and application-specific preparers, synthesizing 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills while reducing recurring per-task expenditure by 82.6%. Rather than directly distilling a default teacher, we evolve the teacher harness and instantiate specialized CUA harnesses to yield high-quality trajectories alongside stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B finally climbs to 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified through different training stages with more efficient reasoning cost, achieving state-of-the-art performance at its parameter size and pushing forward the frontier of on-device intelligence.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Computer-use agents (CUAs) for productivity perceive graphical desktops through screenshots
and act through keyboard and mouse commands. This GUI channel is universal, but it is a
modeling choice rather than a property of the domain, and an expensive one: a typical screenshot
can require thousands of tokens, increasing the cost of processing high-resolution visual input and
grounding interface elements. A person fluent with a computer does not confine themselves to the
mouse: they open a terminal when a terminal is faster and read a file to confirm what a dialog
claims to have saved. Restricting the policy to pixels forces it to re-derive through the GUI what
a single command would accomplish, and removes the most reliable channel it has for checking
its own work. We therefore train a hybrid CUA that acts through two action channels: the GUI
channel, with visual observation and coordinate control, and the terminal channel, a persistent
shell environment in which it may run code, invoke command-line utilities, and call application
libraries directly.
sections.content: Hybrid access does not by itself produce hybrid competence, even for frontier teachers. Prior work shows that access to application tools does not ensure their effective use, and that the same tool set can affect different models differently [1, 2]. The policy must learn which channel is appropriate for the current operation and at what level of abstraction to act. Effective hybrid execution routes each operation to the channel where it fits best: coding and terminal execution for structured files (such as updating spreadsheet with one library call rather than dozens of clicks), and GUI interaction for visual or live application state (such as browser settings that running browser caches in memory and overwrites on exit). Because even frontier models exhibit suboptimal channel routing under naive setup, distilling their default rollouts passes those same limits on to the student. The harness is not neutral container: its tool interfaces, context handling, and guidance directly shape how fixed teacher model acts. Evolving the harness before large-scale rollout elicits stronger hybrid execution than the teacher achieves by default and carries those improvements across the entire training corpus. Moreover, whereas existing pipelines such as ProCUA and ScaleCUA [3, 4] post-train models that already have strong grounding, coding, and agent capabilities, we present an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum starting from general multimodally aligned checkpoint: GUI-oriented midtraining, GUI agent SFT, coding and terminal SFT, hybrid CUA SFT, and online hybrid RL. Sustaining such multi-stage curriculum requires massive, diverse training environments and trajectories, for which we propose the Mage-CUA-Forge environment synthesis pipeline. Unlike prior agent-first approaches that rely on open-ended agent execution to construct each task from scratch, Mage-CUA-Forge uses an authoring agent to construct application-specific preparers and reusable generation workflows tailored to each application and its atomic functionalities, scaling task and environment synthesis with high consistency and low recurring cost. We introduce Mage-VL-Cowork, hybrid CUA trained on 318,837 teacher trajectories over 293,806 synthesized tasks and environments that cover 6,915 atomic skills in an agent-constructed skill taxonomy. Three design decisions define the pipeline: 1. Learning from an evolved hybrid CUA harness. To collect high-quality demonstrations even when frontier teachers default channel routing is imperfect, we evolve the harness including its scaffold, tool interfaces, prompts, and terminal execution environment, before large-scale rollout. Evolution here is as much pruning as growth: unlike skill libraries that continuously accumulate tools [57], we remove overlapping or ill-suited tools so the teacher produces clean hybrid trajectories that yield much larger gains when distilled into the student (3.1, 6.7). Moreover, harness evolution produces specialized configurations with different tool setsincluding GUI harness, terminal harness, and the hybrid CUA harnessallowing us to roll out the same synthesized tasks under multiple harnesses to collect trajectories emphasizing distinct capabilities across our training stages (4). 3 2. single policy that learns the hybrid execution policy. Mage-VL-Cowork observes full-desktop screenshots and emits coordinate mouse and keyboard actions, and in the same episode may execute code and terminal commands on the machine it is operating. The two channels are complementary: pixels are the only channel that reaches spatial, canvas, and renderingdependent state, while code edits at the abstraction the instruction is written in and lets the agent check its work against ground truth rather than against screenshot of dialog. Unlike systems that route between GUI operator and coding operator at the orchestrator level [8, 9], the choice is internal to the policy and is therefore something the training data must teach (3.1). 3. Workflow-first task and environment synthesis. Agent effort is spent once per skill rather than once per task. For each atomic skill, an authoring agent constructs and debugs reusable generation workflow that combines LLM nodes with application-specific preparers, which materialize input artifacts such as Calc workbook or Thunderbird profile with populated mail store. Combined workflows produce task package of instruction, environment setup script, and rubric, and gate nodes check its consistency before the task is accepted. Shared workflows and preparers propagate each improvement across all subsequently generated task instances. Task synthesis, including skill-based generation, has also been studied in terminal settings, where the environment is container filesystem [10, 11]; on full desktop the environment is application state, which is what the preparer exists to produce (3.2). With 4B parameters, Mage-VL-Cowork achieves 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified under 50-step budget, outperforming larger open-source agents including Muse Glimmer-30B (65.9%), Qwen3.627B (63.9%), and EvoCUA-32B (56.7%). Across our curriculum, performance climbs by 20.44 percentage points from GUI SFT (45.56%) through Hybrid SFT (55.84%) to final RL (66.0%), pushing forward practical on-device intelligence for autonomous desktop workflows.

sections.title:
2 Related Work
Computer-use agents and evaluation. GUI grounding methods such as SeeClick [12] learn to
locate interface elements from language instructions. OSWorld [13] and WebVoyager [14] evaluate
the additional requirements of multi-step interaction with desktop and browser environments.
OpenCUA [15] provides open training foundations for computer-use agents. Hybrid approaches
extend visual interaction with coding and terminal actions: CoAct-1 [8] uses an orchestrator to
coordinate GUI and coding agents, whereas our student selects GUI and terminal actions within
a single policy. Tool availability alone does not determine effective channel selection, as also
examined in OSWorld-MCP and controlled screenshot/tool comparisons [1, 2].
sections.content: Synthesized Environment. OS-Genesis [16] constructs GUI trajectories through reverse task synthesis, while CUA-Gym [17] co-generates task instructions, environment states, and reward functions through an adversarial generatordiscriminator loop, and RecreationWorld [18] builds verifiable multi-platform recreation environments for hybrid computer-use agents. For browser environments, InfiniteWeb [19] synthesizes functional websites from specifications, and WebHarbor [20] reconstructs self-hosted website replicas for controllable evaluation and training. Rather than repeating an open-ended agent construction loop for every task, Mage-CUA-Forge uses an authoring agent to build reusable application-specific preparers and skill-conditioned workflows that construct files, application state, and deterministic web replicas at scale. CUA Posttraining. ProCUA [3] and ScaleCUA [4] study scalable computer-use post-training, but start from checkpoints that already possess strong GUI grounding, coding, and agentic capabilities. 3.1 Evolution of the Hybrid Computer-Use Harness
Collecting high-quality hybrid trajectories requires more than a strong frontier model: the teacher
must also select, sequence, and combine GUI actions and terminal commands effectively, a strategy
we call the hybrid execution policy. Under a standard setup, even frontier models show suboptimal
sections.content: 5 channel habitssuch as clicking through repetitive file edits or modifying files on disk that running application caches in memory. Distilling directly from such rollouts passes the teachers default limitations on to the student. We improve the teachers hybrid execution by evolving its external harness while keeping the underlying model weights fixed. We write the teacher agent as AT = (MT , H), = (F, , P, E), (1) where MT is the teacher model and the harness consists of four components. The scaffold organizes the execution loop and context handling. The tool interface exposes the actions of each action channelGUI mouse and keyboard actions and terminal commandstogether with their argument schemas. The prompt , i.e., the system prompt, guides tool use and the hybrid execution policy. The terminal execution environment comprises the command-line utilities and application libraries preinstalled in the Docker sandbox and accessible through the terminal channel. Operational deployments require explicit authorization and sandbox isolation for terminal execution. Harness evolution optimizes , , , and on shared development set. An authoring agent uses rubric-based task success, per-task token cost, execution feedback, and application-level channel statistics to select revisions that improve the successcost trade-off. Harness evolution includes removing redundant tools as well as adding useful ones. Removing xdotool in favor of native screenshot-grounded GUI actions avoids duplicate mouse/keyboard routes and fragile window-focus handling that would split supervision across unequal choices. Conversely, providing domain libraries such as python-pptx in the terminal environment lets the teacher operate directly on slides, shapes, and text runs rather than manually editing unpacked OOXML files. The GUI-and-coding variant achieves higher task success with fewer execution steps than its AX-augmented counterpart; as shown in Section 6.7, this advantage widens into 12.5-percentagepoint gain when distilled into the 4B student. This comparison guides joint optimization of the tool interface and prompt for effective hybrid execution. Figure 3 presents selected teacherharness configurations across channel, scaffold, teacher-model, and prompt refinements. Once selected, the harness remains essentially fixed across subsequent data-generation rounds. We use gpt-5.6-terra as the rubric judge to verify task completion, while trajectory-quality filter retains demonstrations with clean channel routing and tool use. Optimizing the harness before large-scale rollout ensures that captures strong hybrid execution for training (Section 4).

sections.title:
3.2 Workflow-First Task and Environment Generation
A computer-use task package combines an instruction, an executable environment setup, and an
evaluation rubric. Workflow-first generation reuses the construction procedure for these three
coordinated components across task instances.
sections.content: Mage-CUA-Forge builds reusable generation workflow for each atomic skill. Each workflow combines LLM nodes, file preparers, and setup operations. For composite capability, the workflows share unified specification of the requested outcome, required files, and application preconditions, producing coordinated task package. The source-file and setup-script branches share the task specification. Branch-specific checks feed final consistency gate over the complete task package. The workflow routes each required file to preparer appropriate for its type, reusing applicationspecific preparation logic across skill workflows. These preparers materialize the input artifacts needed by the task. Other workflow nodes produce the remaining setup code and combine it with shared setup utilities, such as application launching and desktop-state adjustment. Workflow-specific generation logic is thus separated from reusable file and application preparation, as well as from generic setup operations that are not tied to an individual skill. Dedicated LLM nodes generate the user instruction and its evaluation rubric from the shared specification. Task completion is judged by an LLM against this rubric. Application setup details remain in the setup script, while the instruction describes the users intended outcome. Validation operates at two levels. File-level gates check artifacts against the shared specification, and package-level gate checks consistency among the instruction, setup requirements, and rubric. Gate feedback improves the reusable workflow and shared preparers. Subsequent trajectory evaluation assesses the teachers execution of accepted tasks. Workflow reuse separates one-time construction from recurring generation. LLM nodes supply task-specific content within an established procedure, while shared preparers provide reusable file and application setup logic across skills and task instances. For browser and cross-application workflows, such as retrieving structured records from website and compiling them into spreadsheet or document, live websites introduce anti-bot blocks, content drift, and non-resettable backend state. We therefore pair desktop application preparers with self-hosted, deterministic web environments combining synthesized InfiniteWeb [19] sites and high-fidelity website replicas built upon and extending WebHarbor [20], where each replica resets from local seed database per episode to support verifiable web and cross-application task generation (Appendix A.1).

3.3 Iterative Skill Taxonomy Expansion and Refinement
An exploration agent builds the initial skill taxonomy S by traversing desktop applications and
recording their atomic skills. Rather than keeping S fixed, we refine and expand it across generation
rounds using feedback from student evaluations, adjusting skill granularity, enriching descriptions,
and adding application-specific variations where needed.

sections.title:
3.4 Dataset Statistics
Mage-CUA-Forge produces 293,806 distinct tasks covering 6,915 atomic skills. Single-application
and multi-application tasks account for 61.76% and 38.24%, respectively. Teacher execution and
quality filtering yield 318,837 retained trajectories.
sections.content: The task inventory contains 877,608 taskfile references, counted as distinct extracted paths or filenames within each task. Selected reference families include coding (136,736), spreadsheets (135,805), text or Markdown (134,050), documents (74,052), PDFs (53,996), and presentations (93,784). File references occur in 266,030 tasks (90.5%), averaging 2.99 references per task. The inventory spans 278 suffix categories: 277 named suffixes and one no-extension category. Figure 4 summarizes application involvement and reference families; Appendix defines the counting rules. These synthesized tasks are rolled out under different harness configurations, including the GUI harness, the terminal harness, and the evolved hybrid CUA harness, to collect trajectory data that solve the tasks through different channels and emphasize distinct capabilities for the subsequent training stages described in Section 4. Moreover, we also synthesize the reasoning content before tool call with multi-stage annotation by GPT-5.4-mini. Within the retained hybrid CUA dataset D, supervision covers both execution channels: GUI and terminal actions account for 68.19% and 31.81% of teacher tool calls, respectively.

sections.title:
4 Training Pipeline of Mage-VL-Cowork
Unlike pipelines that post-train checkpoints already specialized for GUI grounding or coding, we
present an end-to-end, progressive five-stage training curriculum starting from an intermediate 4B
Mage-VL checkpoint: (1) GUI-Oriented Midtraining, (2) GUI Agent SFT, (3) Coding & Terminal
SFT, (4) Hybrid CUA SFT, and (5) Online Hybrid RL. This specialize-then-unify curriculum first
builds solid, standalone capabilities in visual grounding, GUI interaction, and coding and terminal
execution before teaching the model to route and combine both channels within a single episode.
sections.content: 8 Context construction and training units. Context folding converts trajectories into turn-level examples, with supervision applied to the next assistant response. Each context retains the three most recent screenshots and four complete responses, while compressing earlier steps into imperative Action: summaries immediately after the system prompt. Each assistant response pairs grounded <think> rationale, concise Action: summary, and the executed <tool_call>; together with the folded Action: history once older screenshots slide out of the window, these structured reasoning, summary, and tool-call traces act as compact working memory, enabling the policy to track prior intent and completed operations across long-horizon, interdependent multi-step tasks (Appendix B.3). sections.title:
4.1 Stage 1: GUI-Oriented Midtraining
We initialize training from an intermediate 4B Mage-VL checkpoint. Evaluating this starting
checkpoint on the core atomic capabilities required for agentic computer use—visual grounding,
chain-of-thought reasoning, and structured tool calling—reveals that all three remain underde-
veloped: the model exhibits an answer-machine tendency [22], defaulting to terse direct replies
rather than reasoning before acting or emitting schema-compliant tool calls. Stage 1 therefore
introduces GUI-oriented midtraining to establish these three atomic capabilities before multi-step
trajectory post-training.
sections.content: Targeting desktop and browser computer use, we curate an OS and web grounding corpus from open-source GUI grounding datasets including UI-E2I-Synth and others [12, 21, 2326], formatting all spatial annotations as computer_use click tool calls and packing same-screenshot queries into shared sequences with target-level deduplication [27]. To jointly acquire screen localization, structured function calling, and chain-of-thought reasoning without mutual interference, we combine this grounding corpus with tool-calling and GUI trajectory data during Stage 1. To monitor whether midtraining checkpoints have acquired these atomic capabilities without waiting for downstream post-training and multi-step rollouts, we construct Single Step Cowork Bench directly from real downstream desktop trajectories, using the target agent action space and system prompt to provide fast diagnostic feedback. Appendix B.1 details our midtraining data design and the two complementary recipes we explored for reconciling non-reasoning grounding 9 supervision with reasoning-annotated tool calls, and Appendix B.2 describes Single Step Cowork Bench.

sections.title:
4.2 Stage 2: GUI Agent SFT
The second stage turns the visual and tool-format foundation into a GUI execution policy. We
collect teacher trajectories with the GUI-only harness. In this setting, task actions are performed
through the GUI channel, and the training examples pair the available screenshot and interaction
history with the teacher’s next action. We use these trajectories to fine-tune the midtrained
checkpoint on complete computer-use workflows.
sections.content: GUI trajectories connect single-step grounding to multi-step interaction, teaching the model which control to operate next, when to scroll, how to enter text, and how to continue after the interface changes. Building strong standalone GUI execution first ensures that when the model later learns hybrid channel routing, it chooses between two capable channels rather than routing around weak visual policy.

sections.title:
4.3 Stage 3: Coding & Terminal SFT
The third stage develops coding and terminal execution capabilities, including terminal operation,
code generation, repository navigation, and debugging with Terminal-Bench-style [28] and SWE-
bench-style training data [29].
sections.content: We combine general software-engineering data with desktop terminal harness trajectories from productivity tasks we synthesized in Section 3. While repository-level tasks cover source files, tests, and build tools, desktop coding trajectories teach the model to read and modify workbooks, documents, presentations, and application state using specialized Python libraries and commandline utilities. Specifically, we run terminal-only teacher harness on the same batch of desktop tasks used for GUI trajectory collection in Stage 2. Retaining the successful coding and terminal trajectories alongside general terminal and software-engineering data gives the student direct examples of how to solve target desktop tasks through code before Stage 4 combines both channels.

sections.title:
4.4 Stage 4: Hybrid CUA SFT
Stage 4 brings the visual and coding foundations together by training on the 318,837 trajectories
collected under the evolved hybrid harness (Section 3.1). Within a shared task context, a single
policy learns turn-level channel routing—deciding when to act through the GUI, when to use
coding and terminal execution, and when to switch between them, such as using code to edit a
structured file and then returning to the application window to inspect the rendered result.
sections.content: Because 4B model is sensitive to noisy or ambiguous demonstrations, optimizing the teacher harness for both task success and token efficiency and filtering trajectories before training, which is critical. Rather than merely exposing the student to larger tool inventory, the resulting supervision directly teaches effective channel routing and compact execution. The final supervised stage draws on the 318,837 retained hybrid trajectories; the final hybrid dataset contains 1,377,805 packed bins. The resulting model combines the visual grounding and GUI execution learned in the first two stages, the general and desktop-specific coding capabilities developed in the third, and the hybrid execution policy demonstrated by the evolved hybrid agent. We refer to the checkpoint obtained after this stage as Mage-VL-Cowork-SFT.

sections.title:
4.5 Stage 5: Online Hybrid RL
The final stage refines Mage-VL-Cowork-SFT with online reinforcement learning in the hybrid
harness. We train on the 1,988 tasks released by ScaleCUA [4], each paired with a verifiable reward.
Following ScaleCUA, we use frontier sampling, with task weights based on pre-run success rates to
allocate rollouts toward the learning frontier. The policy is optimized with GRPO [30]. Rollouts
sections.content: 10 are generated asynchronously with bounded policy staleness, and we apply vanilla truncated importance sampling (TIS) [31] to correct the mismatch between the rollout and training policies. Each rollout uses the same step budget as our OSWorld-Verified evaluation. The resulting model is Mage-VL-Cowork, which we evaluate in Section 6. Each optimizer update admits 96 task groups with eight episode slots per group. four-batch admission window bounds policy lag at three updates, and TIS caps importance weights at 2.0. Mixed-policy episodes are enabled. CPU workers execute desktop environments, while GPU services handle training and inference. The relay carries control, inference, and compact trajectories; weight synchronization uses an intra-GPU-cluster path. Section 5 summarizes the architecture; Appendix gives the implementation details, runtime profile, and measurement definitions.

sections.title:
5.1 Workload Characteristics and Design Requirements
Desktop rollouts combine inference with application loading, content entry, and state updates.
Individual observed episodes exceed 40 minutes, motivating asynchronous scheduling so that
completed tasks can advance training independently of long-running episodes.
sections.content: The resource requirements are also heterogeneous. Desktop environments need CPU capacity, guest memory, and nested virtualization, whereas model inference and optimization run on GPUs. For compact model on B200 hardware, environment execution and orchestration can remain important latency sources even when individual model calls are relatively fast. We consequently manage environment capacity separately from model-serving and training capacity, and use asynchronous rollouts rather than requiring lockstep progress across the desktop fleet. Visual rollouts create repeated screenshot inputs across turn-level examples. sections.content: WebVoyager-Static. Evaluating browser agents on live websites [14] is confounded by both environment instability and unreliable grading: page content varies across time and location, antibot checks and access blocks interrupt rollouts, VLM judges lack backend ground truth and often credit unverified claims absent from the final screenshot, and newer models already know much of the target information and tend to guess answers without browsing. To construct high-fidelity offline benchmark, we build on WebHarbor [20] and substantially expand its self-hosted replicas, reconstructing the missing pages, interactive controls, and local database records required to faithfully support all 643 tasks across the 15 WebVoyager [14] sites. Rather than relying on final-screenshot VLM judge alone, grading verifies both the execution trace, by confirming that the agent visited the target pages and performed the required UI operations, and the final outcome, by checking the agents answer and backend database state against ground truth. This deterministic setup eliminates the score inflation common on live web benchmarks  (Table 4)  while running at 12 fraction of the cost of full desktop VM rollouts, making WebVoyager-Static an effective multi-step diagnostic for validating our web data and iterating on early post-training checkpoints. sections.content: Comparing previously published live WebVoyager scores against our offline evaluation reveals drop of 12.8 to 33.1 percentage points across the five models with self-reported live results [21, 35, 36]. Auditing the rollout traces under both the original live-judge protocol and our offline verifier shows why: because the standard live judge inspects only the final screenshot and explicitly instructs the evaluator to trust unsupported claims in the agents text (choose to believe the content), it rewards fluent guessing and masks three recurring failure modes in current web agents: (1) shortcut answering from search snippets or parametric memory, where agents answer after few steps from result card or prior knowledge without opening the detail page that holds the ground-truth evidence; (2) incomplete multi-constraint filtering, where agents locate the target site and issue keyword query but fail to operate interactive filter controls (such as date pickers, price sliders, or sort menus), returning the first plausible candidate that violates secondary constraints; and (3) uncommitted stateful interactions, where agents fill out forms or click preliminary buttons and declare success while the backend database records no actual mutation (e.g., an empty cart or unsubmitted booking). These findings suggest that screenshot-only judging can inadvertently incentivize premature, persuasive answers over thorough interaction. sections.content: A.1 High-Fidelity Web Replicas Figure 9 Construction and reset of web replica. Reference structure, assets, and records are combined with generated content to assemble the local site. Each episode operates on working database restored from the read-only seed. The website and records are illustrative. To support the controllable browser workflows and offline evaluations introduced in Sections 3.2 and 6.1, we pair synthesized InfiniteWeb [19] environments with self-hosted website replicas built upon and expanding WebHarbor [20] (Figure 9). Each replica runs as local Flask and SQLite service with target domains routed to the local host. Before every episode, the environment restores fresh working database from read-only seed snapshot, isolating stateful operations across rollouts while exposing the underlying tables for deterministic verification. Constructing and upgrading these replicas follows two core principles: Frontend and interactive fidelity. Early mock environments often simplify pages into generic templates or static placeholder blocks, which reduces visual complexity and omits the controls needed for multi-step tasks. To match real-world interfaces, we capture reference snapshots from target websitesspanning DOM hierarchies, computed CSS rules, and static assets (logos, icons, and inline SVGs), supplemented by web archives when live endpoints are restrictedand reconstruct the full page structure. Beyond static layout, we implement the interactive controls required for end-to-end task completion, including multi-attribute filter panels, date pickers, sorting menus, pagination, stateful submission forms, and domain-specific components such as Leaflet maps and Chart.js views. Database grounding and multimodal completion. We populate each replicas seed database primarily from authentic structured sources, including public APIs and data dumps (e.g., ESPN, Stack Exchange, Hacker News, and OpenStreetMap), web crawl archives, and bibliographic catalogs. When raw records lack full-text bodies, detailed item descriptions, or image assets, we condition LLM text generation and image-generation models on the authentic structured attributes to synthesize coherent articles, descriptions, and context-matched thumbnails. All synthesized presentation fields are tagged separately from the canonical attributes queried by task verifiers, ensuring realistic visual and textual density without introducing ambiguity into ground-truth grading. A.2 Web Task Synthesis and Verifiable Contracts Figure 10 Structured task synthesis and contract compilation. The illustrative example links database predicates, navigation path, and compositional skill graph to shared task specification. The instruction renderer receives only public query constraints; the verifier compiler uses the private target to check page visits and final database state. Building on the resettable replicas in Appendix A.1, we formulate web task generation as structured synthesis pipeline that pairs every synthesized instruction with an executable verification contract (Figure 10). Each replica exposes its seed relational database D0, site navigation graph = (V, E) over page templates and UI transitions, and set of stateful backend operations. From these structured representations, we construct task specifications through three complementary approaches: 1. Database-grounded query synthesis. We sample target records and multi-attribute filter predicates directly from the seed database D0 and execute an SQL query over D0 to ensure that the resulting constraint set yields unique, non-trivial answer before turning the predicates into user task. 2. Navigation-path synthesis. We sample executable multi-hop walks over the sites pagetransition graph (e.g., Home Category Listing Filtered Results Item Detail Saved Collection), converting each valid path into goal-directed task whose required intermediate pages and terminal state are known by construction. 3. Compositional skill workflows. Extending the workflow-first principle from Section 3.2 to browser environments, we abstract recurring web operations into typed meta-skills such as keyword search, multi-attribute filtering, comparative ranking, and stateful form submissioneach equipped with explicit preconditions and postconditions. Composing compatible meta-skills into directed acyclic workflows across distinct entities in D0 produces diverse multi-step tasks that share reusable verification template. Contract compilation and targeted curriculum expansion. Each task specification compiles along two separated branches (Figure 10, right). To render natural-language instructions without leaking ground-truth answers into the prompt, we enforce strict information asymmetry: the instruction-rendering LLM receives only the public query constraints and allowed filter attributes, while the private target records and oracle answers remain withheld; candidate prompts that fail uniqueness or naturalness checks are discarded. In parallel, the verifier compiler binds the private 20 target records to deterministic checks over both the execution trace (confirming required page visits and UI actions) and the final outcome (checking the submitted answer and post-episode SQLite state). Following the iterative feedback loop in Section 3.3, subsequent synthesis rounds increase sampling weight on skill compositions where the student policy underperformssuch as multi-constraint filtering or detail-page evidence verificationsupplying rule-verified browser and cross-application trajectories for post-training. A.3 Dataset Counting Definitions Tasks are deduplicated across 11 batches by domain and task identifier. taskfile reference is distinct path or filename extracted from tasks metadata or text, including declared outputs. References are counted within each task, with corresponding structured and textual declarations merged when resolved. Application coverage is multi-label, totaling 419,505 applicationtask incidences across nine application categories. The 17,542 InfiniteWeb [19] tasks are reported separately. File categories are defined by extracted suffixes, including custom suffixes and no-extension category. Midtraining Explorations, Context Design, and Compute Accounting B.1 GUI Midtraining Design Trade-Offs Figure 11 Three design choices in Stage 1 GUI-oriented midtraining: (1) decoupling the click-only grounding prompt from the full agent schema to prevent action-space collapse, (2) deduplicating repeated target elements within packed single-screenshot sequences to eliminate in-context coordinate copying, and (3) selectively masking interior <think> tokens to balance reasoning format retention with grounding and tool-syntax learning. Building on the Stage 1 overview in Section 4.1, Figure 11 illustrates three design choices that proved critical when jointly training screen grounding, structured tool calling, and chain-of-thought reasoning. Domain-targeted grounding and system-prompt decoupling. We curate our grounding pool from open-source GUI datasets, including UGround [23], UI-E2I-Synth [24], OS-Atlas [25], MolmoWeb [21], JEDI [26], and SeeClick [12], filtering for 720p1080p desktop and browser screenshots and normalizing all bounding boxes to center coordinates in [0, 999] formatted as computer_use click tool calls. We pair these click-only examples with minimal grounding system prompt declaring only "enum": ["click"] (Figure 11, left). Training click-only grounding data under the full 10-action agent prompt causes the policy to associate the full prompt with unconditional clicking and ignore type, scroll, or keypress downstream; decoupling the two prompts transfers visual localization without collapsing the action space. Target-level deduplication in same-screenshot packing. Packing multiple grounding queries for the same screenshot into shared sequence [27] avoids repeated image encoding. However, opensource grounding datasets often contain multiple paraphrased queries targeting the same UI element on screenshot (Figure 11, center). When packed together, later turns achieve near-zero loss by copying the coordinate pair emitted for an earlier turn (Ak = Aj) instead of attending to the image. Retaining at most one query per distinct target location per screenshot removes this shortcut and drives the steady grounding gains in Figure 6. In packed sequences, grounding Reconciling non-reasoning grounding with reasoning tool calls. example averages only 33 supervised action tokens, whereas reasoning-annotated tool-call example averages 575 supervised tokens, 69% of which belong to the <think> block (Figure 11, right). Unmasked supervision lets verbose reasoning dominate gradients and dilute localization, whereas stripping <think> blocks causes the model to drop reasoning tags at test time. We explored two complementary recipes: 1. Selective <think>-body masking on tool-call blends. We mask the interior tokens of the <think> reasoning while supervising the opening and closing <think>...</think> delimiter tags and the <tool_call>, preserving the think-then-act format at inference time while focusing gradients on tool syntax and coordinates. 2. Incorporating post-training GUI trajectories into midtraining. We also explored mixing synthesized multi-step GUI trajectories directly into Stage 1 alongside grounding data, exposing the model early to the full downstream action space and step-level rationales. Both recipes reach comparable accuracy after downstream SFT; we adopt selective <think>-body masking for the main pipeline because it keeps Stage 1 decoupled from trajectory synthesis, uses fewer tokens, and iterates faster. B.2 Single Step Cowork Bench Standard function-calling benchmarks such as BFCL evaluate text-only tool use without visual inputs, standard GUI grounding benchmarks test only single-action coordinate clicking, and end-to-end desktop benchmarks such as OSWorld require downstream SFT and hours of multi-step VM rollouts per checkpoint. To jointly evaluate visual localization, action-type selection, and reasoning format during Stage 1 midtraining, we construct Single Step Cowork Bench from 342 representative interaction steps sampled from real desktop trajectories across office suites (Calc, Writer, Impress), web browsing (Chrome), media and creative tools (GIMP, VLC), development environments (VS Code), and system utilities. Every example is evaluated under the full downstream agent system prompt and spans eight GUI action primitives (click, double_click, triple_click, drag, scroll, type, keypress, and terminate). To separate direct localization from intent-driven reasoning, each step is paired with both an explicit instruction (naming the target control directly, e.g., Click the Settings menu item in the popup menu) and an intent instruction (stating the local subgoal, e.g., Open the VS Code settings page from this menu). Grading jointly verifies (1) valid <think> and <tool_call> syntax, (2) exact action-type and argument match, and (3) spatial hit accuracy within the groundtruth bounding box. During Stage 1 development, this lightweight diagnostic surfaced failure modes invisible to click-only grounding benchmarksincluding action-space collapse onto click under the full agent prompt, hallucinated placeholder function names (example_function_name) 22 copied from the schema, and unterminated or missing <think> blocks on dense spreadsheet viewsallowing rapid recipe iteration before multi-step post-training. B.3 Context Window Design and Step-Level Reasoning Synthesis Figure 12 Sliding-window context design and step-level rationale synthesis: (1) each turn conditions on folded imperative Action: summaries of steps 1 . . . 4 together with the three most recent visual turns (t 3, 2, 1), (2) retaining three screenshots exposes whether prior actions altered the interface and prevents repetitive no-op click loops, and (3) reasoning synthesis pass grounds first-person <think> traces and Action: summaries on before/after screenshots and the executed tool call. Long-horizon desktop trajectories face fundamental context trade-off: retaining every historical screenshot quickly exhausts the context budget, whereas keeping only the current screenshot alongside text history leaves the policy blind to whether its previous action actually changed the screen. In early iterations with ten text turns and single screenshot, slightly off-target click that left the interface unchanged frequently triggered repetitive click loops (Figure 12, bottom left). To resolve this, each turn-level training example uses an asymmetric sliding window (Figure 12, top): it retains the three most recent visual turns (t 3, 2, 1) with their screenshots and full assistant responses so the model can directly verify before-and-after UI transitions, while folding earlier steps (1 . . . 4) into single-line imperative Action: summaries that preserve compact long-horizon record of completed operations. To supply consistent supervision for both in-window reasoning and out-of-window history folding across heterogeneous trajectory sources, we run step-level reasoning synthesis pass conditioned on the task context, before/after screenshots, and the executed tool call (Figure 12, bottom right). For every step, this pass produces uniform three-part target: (1) grounded first-person <think> rationale, (2) concise imperative Action: summary that directly serves as the folded memory entry once the turn slides past 3, and (3) the verified <tool_call>. Together with the asymmetric window, this uniform output format turns the models own generations into self-sustaining working memory across SFT and RL rollouts: recent turns provide visual and reasoning context for local error recovery, while earlier Action: lines accumulate into compact execution log across long-horizon, interdependent tasks. RL Infrastructure Details and Measurements This appendix describes the RaaS implementation and deployment, followed by workload, transport, update-timing, and policy-lag profiles. Each profile is associated with its measurement run, update window, and aggregation rule. C.1 Rollout-as-a-Service Architecture The infrastructure integrates PoLar [32], Slime, Azure Relay, and Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS). The training client uses Slime adapters for desktop rollouts, turn-level samples, and data-parallel shards. SGLang [33] serves model requests, while RaaS workers on Azure VMSS run the resource manager and CUA runners. Routing and image preparation execute on CPUs; inference and optimization execute on GPUs. The relay exposes three logical communication channels: Control. The training client submits work and queries task status and ready manifests from the resource manager. Inference. The harness sends prompts and screenshots to the inference service and receives generated tokens and log probabilities. Bulk trajectories. Stored compact episodes are delivered to the training adapters using deduplication and gzip compression. The relay carries control, inference, and compact-trajectory traffic. Trainer-to-inference weight synchronization and training collectives use intra-cluster paths. External judge calls and artifact storage use their respective service interfaces. C.2 Resource Management and Sandbox Execution The resource manager contains three components. The Task Dispatcher handles submission, queueing, dispatch, status, and ready manifests. The Sandbox Scheduler manages fleet capacity and sandbox allocation and release, with separate admission limits for initialization, running, and post-run processing. The Compact Episode JSON Store gathers completed trajectory records and supplies the bulk-transfer path. These components separate task coordination and environment capacity from the model-serving process. 24 Each host has separate concurrency caps for sandbox initialization, execution, and post-run processing: 4 (INIT), 16 (RUN), and 8 (POSTRUN), respectively. Lifecycle-specific admission control manages setup and post-processing alongside the 16 running-episode slots. Each CUA runner contains four components. EnvRuntime provides the desktop environment, captures screenshots, and executes actions. CUAHarness maintains the stateful agent loop, issues model requests, and dispatches GUI or terminal tools. Evaluator produces the tasks evaluation, reward, and termination outcomes, using rule-based checks or an external judge where required. TrajectoryBuilder combines turn traces and evaluator outcomes into compact episode JSON for transfer to the training client. C.3 Asynchronous Rollouts and Trajectory Preparation The configured update batch contains 96 task groups with eight episode slots per group, or 768 slots. The admission window spans four batches, with maximum configured policy lag of three optimizer updates. This organization allows rollout collection and optimization to overlap while bounding the policy-version gap of admitted data. Mixed-policy episodes are enabled. TIS caps importance weights at 2.0. Admission is configured over four-batch window, with policy lag bounded at three optimizer updates (Section 4.5). The data path keeps compact trajectories separate from expanded training tensors. The rollout bridge and adapters construct per-turn samples and data-parallel shards. Ray distributes compressed images, tokens, and metadata; node-local CPU processing decodes and resizes the images and applies the models image processor before the tensors are consumed by the trainer GPUs. Prefetching prepares trajectory data ahead of training consumption rather than placing every preparation operation on the immediate update path. Each turn retains up to three recent images. Compact episodes deduplicate stored screenshots for transfer, and turn-level preparation materializes the image inputs required by each training example. C.4 Deployment Scale and Runtime Profile The CPU fleet comprises 70 Standard_D64d_v5 hosts, each with 64 vCPUs and 256 GiB of memory. Sixteen GUI slots per host provide 1,120 configured slots. Each guest receives eight vCPUs and 4 GiB of memory, giving 2:1 guest-to-host vCPU allocation ratio. The reference GPU deployment uses 32 B200 GPUs, split into 24 training and eight inference GPUs. deployment with 28 training GPUs and four inference GPUs reached peak occupancy of 1,120 running environments. The 24/8 split is the reference configuration used in the architecture diagram. Figure 13 Runtime profile of policy lag. In the workload-profiling window, each update prepares 18,437.56 turn sequences, 34,973.68 image occurrences, and 136.49 million language-model tokens on average.
